utterances.text: Is that the conclusion that you spoke about?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN MISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, is it the same document, Mr. Lukic, I see the emblem on the top is different, and I don't see on the right document, the writing that is written next to the emblem on the left.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yeah, it's just the translators probably were not able to put that emblem on the right-hand side but the translation is as can you see even on the left-hand side there is a text, missing persons institute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can we see 1D5438 now, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Before we do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Okay. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: This document in both versions has not been filled. How do we get to the conclusion when we don't know when the meeting of the verification was held, who signed it? It is just a form.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It's just a form.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This gentleman told us that that process has not been started yet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So now if we can get 1D5438, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We see before us a document. Could you please tell us what it is about.

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN MISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a report of the head of sector, and he indicates to us certain problems in the process of verification, and he is asking us to redress that. I don't know what this document exactly refers to. It's probably lack of personnel or due to certain technical problems, the work of the commission has been slowed down, or maybe there is a lack of certain documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can we look at the next page now, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Please don't touch the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But the witness touched the screen so, please, if the page can be fixed. Okay. And can we see the last page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Who is Mr. Simun Novakovic, that is to say, the person who signed this document?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN MISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Simun Novakovic is the chief of sector of the central records of missing persons of Bosnia-Herzegovina and that is one of the sectors in the institute for missing persons of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We see that August 2010 is the date of the document and Mr. Novakovic is indicating certain shortcomings. Could you just tell us what Mr. Simun Novakovic's ethnic background is?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN MISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He belongs to the Croat people.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now take a look at 1D5439, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Are you familiar with this document?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN MISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is also a report of the chief of sector, and it is from the month of July 2010.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Again, this is Mr. Simun Novakovic?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN MISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What is the system of decision-making in your institute?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN MISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At all levels, where a commission operates, the system is by consensus. In this case, for the verification commission, there is supposed to be consensus on the part of all three members of the commission or, if they are speaking about the collegium, then all three members of the collegium have to reach consensus.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I would just like to show you the law now, the Law on Missing Persons. We've already looked at it. It is -- I didn't write down the D number but it was 1D5450. [In English] From ...

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Actually, we need D1094. This one has translation. I apologise. We need page 3, paragraph 5. I think in both versions. No. Next page, sorry. Page 4. Obviously I had a different version. So it is still paragraph 5 but the last -- Article 5 but the last paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We see that in the last paragraph it says --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You're reading, Mr. Lukic. Could you slowly start reading again.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I will. Thank you. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So this is what the paragraph says. I quote: "Officials with duties related to the tracing of missing persons cannot carry out this duty if they are members of steering and other boards, or executive bodies, of political parties, or if they are politically engaged representatives, and must not follow political party instructions." [In English] Can we go into the private session for a while.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're back in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let's clear up one thing that may not be quite clear. How many persons have been verified so far, contrary to the law?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And how many persons have been properly verified?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN MISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Around 7.000.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Does this finalize the process of verification?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN MISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Has the procedure been finalized for these irregularly verified 10.100 or 10.200?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN MISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, because they are irregular, it can't be finalised.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What needs to be done?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN MISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To restart the process of verification, according to legal procedures, the way it was prescribed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: These 10.100 or 10.200, what do they have in common? Why were they processed in the way they were? What's the common denominator between them?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN MISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there are two main common denominators. First of all, they were verified only based on the minutes on identification. And, second, for the most part, it's mainly persons from the PIP who were verified at that stage, the Identification Project of Podrinje. And as the reports were coming in, these persons were verified.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Among this number of people who were verified in that way, are any related to the events in Srebrenica 95?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN MISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe they form the majority. I mean, I don't believe; I know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In total, after the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina, how many persons were reported missing?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN MISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to the records received at the institute, around 34.000 names were registered. By integrating these databases, we came to a clearer number, arriving at a total of around 32.000.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Were there any cases where people were recorded as missing, whereas, in reality, they were dead?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN MISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What can be done in such cases? Tell me.

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN MISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unfortunately, nothing.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Why?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN MISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you've seen a minute ago, there could be perfectly fair reasons. A person died, it wasn't known, et cetera. However, based on certain reports that had not undergone our process, courts had, in some cases, already issued their decisions and entered these persons into the registers of death, and, thus, it was set in stone, so to speak.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But I'm trying to understand this in view of the -- one of the earlier questions. Were there any cases where people were recorded as missing whereas, in reality, they were dead? Were you thinking, Mr. Lukic, in terms, in reality, of the administrative reality, that is, that they were declared dead or you were referring to a reality that means, physically, they were established as having died? Which of the two are we talking about?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I think my question was they were considered to be missing and actually they died.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Died physically.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: They died physically. Not killed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, if you are killed you die as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yeah but [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... not living anymore.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In B/C/S, when you say [B/C/S spoken], this is considered that somebody died of illness or natural causes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I want to know exactly what this evidence now is about and perhaps could you --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Okay --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- take it up again so that no unclarity remains.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But Judge Fluegge suggests that you would do that after the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And I will follow him. Mr. Misic, we'll take a break. We'd like to see you back in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We resume at 20 minutes past 12.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the -- Mr. Tieger, you're on your feet. I was about to ask the usher to escort the witness into the courtroom. How would -- how much time would you need to address us.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: It's about one minute, I expect two minutes maybe. It doesn't need to be done now if the Court is concerned but I can probably do it with the [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... meanwhile the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: It concerns the next witness, Mr. President, Mr. Tusevljak and a scheduling issue that doesn't affect this week's discussed but does have implications for further scheduling. In connection with his proposed upcoming testimony the Defence propose to use a 248-page document which unfortunately, through administrative oversight that I know from discussions surprised even Mr. Lukic, was only provided to the Prosecution Monday afternoon and with no translation. Mr. Lukic agrees that under these circumstances it precludes the use of the document with the witness at this time. And he has advised of his intention to have the witness return to address the document in due course and no earlier than 20 days after the interpretation -- English translation of the document is received and has been provided to the Prosecution. We have no objection to that approach. I bring it to the attention the Court because we don't regard such matters as being only party matters although I imagine that this will meet with the Court's approval, particularly since it's highly unlikely that the witness would conclude his testimony this week in any event and would therefore have to return at a later time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I also note that the Prosecution has expressed some relevance and provenance concerns about the document but consider that those should be best deferred until the translation has been received and since this document ostensibly concerns Serb deaths in -- civilian deaths in Sarajevo and the parties are moving increasingly close to the agreement the Court asked us to pursue about the minimum, at least the minimum number of Serb civilians killed in Sarajevo, it may be the case that this issue is largely resolved before the witness would need to return in any event. That's what I wanted to advise the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In view of the ongoing conversations between the parties and the partly solution of the problem, the Chamber, at this moment, I think, but I'm looking at my colleagues, would not intervene, and just accept the commonly shared way of proceeding.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I just wanted to ask my colleague, if they want Mr. Sasa Lukic to work in direct examination on the document so they are completely prepared for cross later on or they want not to have the direct examination regarding that document either.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I appreciate the inquiry -- I would ask the attorney handling the witness about that. I think there are pros and cons either way but I grateful appreciate the inquiry and I'll get back to Mr. Lukic shortly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, at this moment the Chamber sees no reason to intervene and it's most likely will also accept what you have agreed upon in this respect. Then if that was it, Mr. Tieger -- Mr. Misic, apologies for ignoring you entering the courtroom and continuing with some administrative matters, but Mr. Lukic will now pay further attention to your knowledge. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I know that I'm close or I already used my time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think you did already --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I will ask you for additional -- probably half an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, the Chamber is -- if you could try to keep it as short as possible, the Chamber is aware that it intervenes very often. At the same time, it cannot be said that the way in which the evidence was presented and the absence of some documents, et cetera, has not contributed to the frequency of those interventions. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Misic, do you personally insist on finding out the reasons for disappearance?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN MISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, that's our legal obligation. Not the reasons but the cause of disappearance.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What are the reasons why you insist on establishing the cause of disappearance?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN MISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, in order for the search to be successful it's logical to start from where the person went missing, when, and under what circumstances. If the central records, that is to say, the verification had the purpose of establishing the causes of disappearance, the only way is to start from these three questions. That's one. And the second. How can we contribute to finding out the truth for the sake of the family? To stop with manipulating these three pieces of information. Until each person has a complete case file so that it's no longer a missing person but a person who was once alive, who had a certain course of life, and to close the file so that nobody can manipulate where the facts about that person. If we cannot achieve that, then we shouldn't exist in the first place.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What, in fact, do you verify?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN MISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We verify the general details about the person and we determine -- I mean, the commission determines the time, place, and circumstances of disappearance. But before that, we have to determine beyond any dispute that this person was once alive, that he or she was a national of Bosnia-Herzegovina, that they really went missing, and then the rest that I mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In your work, did you deal with the ICMP database?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN MISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The ICMP is one of the databases that were incorporated into the database of missing persons. It's very useful, but it's also incomplete and it contains inaccuracies, errors, substantial errors, and another reason why we had to deal with it is that we - I mean, the commission, although they began with it even before I joined the commission - we took over the ICMP database as a basis for creating our base of verified data, and we frequently come across situations when you incorporate unverified or inaccurate information, and all we end up with is what the ICMP has managed to find out, and we have no real circumstances or dates of disappearance, for instance.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is there a document that prescribes how the process of verification should proceed?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN MISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We have three documents. First of all, the missing persons law; then the rules on the verification of central records; and, third, the guide-lines adopted by the collegium for the work of verification commissions.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can we see 1D5442, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: While we're waiting for it, if you find any error in the ICMP database, do you report that and together with the reasons why you think that it's an error to the ICMP?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Any base can have mistakes and it does.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's the beginning of my question. That's taken. Do you report any error you find in the ICMP database to the ICMP so that they can consider to possibly correct -- you don't do that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. You've answered my question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can I ask a question also. Sir, in your previous answer this is page 52, lines 11 to the end you say: "We took over the ICMP database as a basis of creating our base of verified data, and we frequently come across situations where you incorporate unverified or inaccurate information and all we end up with is what the ICMP has managed to find out and we have no real circumstances or dates of disappearance, for instance." Now if the ICMP is taken as the basis for your data and you get to a situation where you have no real circumstances or dates does it then mean, in fact, that your own data, therefore, is as incomplete as the ICMP is incomplete?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Our base cannot be incomplete. That is to say, if we enter data about a particular person, what is verified was verified. What exists in the base and has not been verified does not exist for us until the verification commission establishes what the situation is. So if there is a discrepancy or if something cannot be proven then that person is registered as unverified and is removed from the base actually not physically removed from the base but not verified. So that is the base. I don't know if I'm being clear. So.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... clear to me. Are you saying that the data you get from ICMP that ICMP purports that that data is verified? Or is it just a missing person who must still be investigated? What data do you get from ICMP?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The ICMP does not have a verified base. It's a working base, just like all other bases so there is no verified ICMP base.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... I'm asking you about and therefore because they don't have a verified data and you use their data as the base and it is incomplete and if you don't have any other sources of information then your data is logically going to be incomplete. Am I right? Unless you're telling me that you get data from elsewhere to supplement the ICMP one.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When Mr. Lukic asked whether I dealt with the ICMP base earlier on I have to explain this. Our register of verified persons is entered into the work base of the ICMP. Now if our verification commission does not enter into that base all the necessary information, and does not verify all the information, then one gets a false picture, a false impression. For example, for the first 10.000 persons, only the name, surname and -- have been verified and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... you are not answering my question, so let's leave it at that. I think we are at cross-purposes; we probably don't understand each other.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Misic, just tell us, I don't think that you answered this question actually. What are the sources on the basis of which you work. Is that only the ICMP base?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN MISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We have the so-called four primary bases but then there is all this other knowledge and all these other records that we may obtain. To this day, it is possible to give a new base to our centre and that can be use, for verification. So first of all is information that was received from the ICRC so it's the Red Cross base. Then the base of the Federal Commission for Missing Persons. Then the base of the commission for Republika Srpska for missing persons and then the fourth one is the ICMP base. So these are the so-called four primary bases and they are the foundation for cross-referencing data in order to establish what the law requires to be established for missing persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Apart from these four, you say there are other sources as well. Do give us some examples, briefly outside these four bases. What are your other sources of information and knowledge?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN MISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Wherever there is any kind of discrepancy, we have to look at official records from other institutions, from birth registers, death registers, and so on. So this is information about persons in different institutions. Then, also, it is possible, and I've already said that this is also obligatory, to check whether the person had been registered before the war and in what status it is today. For example, if a person asked for a document from the war, then that person has to be alive. Then also there are voters' registers from the previous period and then there are also records that --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you say a document from the war or after the war?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN MISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Documents that --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do they obtain documents after the war or before the war and then you say that if somebody got a document during the war, then they must be alive after the war.

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN MISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I meant if a person was getting a personal ID after 1996 that means that that person is alive and, for example, that person is registered as missing in our lists.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What is relevant for the rules of procedure for the commission of verification of information?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN MISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This procedure, to prepare all documents so that this documentation is checked, as I've already explained, that all three members of the commission should reach agreement that that is that, and then the legal minimum should be established about that person, and then, later on, a conclusion will be drawn.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We see that that commission is part of your institute; right?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN MISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just briefly, let us take look at document 1D5453, please. Could you please tell us what kind of document this is.

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN MISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this is a document from 2013 that I wrote because, as I've already said -- well, I sent it to the International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia, The Hague, Netherlands. I wrote it, as I mentioned a moment ago that there is this parallel institute where my colleague Masovic is then there is documentation there and I don't know about it, and as a rule, we make all our documents in three copies and all members of the commission have to receive it. Then also if there is a inquiry then that should be sent to the headquarters of the institute and I provide the address there and it shouldn't be sent just to my colleague Mr. Masovic's office. I saw that there was documentation that was not reaching the headquarters of the institute. And then the institute was responding to that documentation and that's not proper, you see. It is impossible for any of the three of us to receive documents without going through the required protocol, and no one can write a reply without giving the draft to the other two colleagues. However, sometimes this procedure was not followed. And that's why I wrote. Because I found out that some documentation was reaching the wrong address.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You say impossible. Well, obviously it's possible but is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN MISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, it's possible, but it is not right, precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D5436, could we briefly take a look at that as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could -- apparently then documentation was sent, not in the proper way by one of the members of the board. Do we know whether that was in any way used? Because it only is relevant if that information is both wrong and, second, then, though being wrong, being used.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It's the next document, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's the next document.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Jeremy.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Your Honours, yesterday I indicated to you that 193 missing persons certificates were used as a source in Ewa Tabeau's municipalities proof of death report so of the certificates that were sent to us, 193 of those were referenced in her report and there are an additional 30 certificates that have been bar tabled and that's the entirety of the certificates relied on pursuant to the correspondence referred to here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Which then, of course, makes it very relevant to know whether these were properly verified or not properly verified cases. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Just to add, as I said yesterday, they were never used as a single source in Ms. Tabeau's report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What we have before us is the first page of three that I have in this set under this number, Dr. Simun Novakovic, a Ph.D. holder, is writing to you.

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN MISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I repeat once again. I don't know how many documents like this were written and how many requests of this kind were sent. This one I came across by accident. Documents had to be done in the central records of the institute, and it is only within the sector's purview to prepare such documents. However, if the chief of sector says that something was not done in the sector, then the sector does not stand by that and how can I stand by that then? I cannot say that the information there is untrue but, unfortunately, that is the procedure. I don't know what was sent, what was not sent. I cannot stand by such a document. The chief of sector cannot stand by such a document. It's an illegal document.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can we see the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jeremy, is there any way for you to find out knowing this name, whether that was one certificate used.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. That was one of the certificates used and my understanding is that on the basis of the sources of which this was one, Ms. Tabeau's conclusion was inconclusive.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Inconclusive, so it is not in way supporting the Prosecution's case, in relation to this person.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And I don't know if we have to go through all this. Apparently --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It's the last document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We see --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... document.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're not going to mention the name. We see here the certificate is issued for the purpose of regulating, et cetera, and it is for the case of General Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN MISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the chief of sector disassociated himself from this document -- I mean, from such documents, whether this was processed at the CEN or not he is saying that it wasn't. So I'm not going to speak about the content of the certificate whether it is correct or not correct but it is illegal.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let us briefly look at the last page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we do so, could you tell us whether you recognise the signature on this document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that is the signature of my colleague, Amor Masovic, and the stamp is the stamp of our institute for missing persons in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And you've never seen the request referred to, the request by the Office of the Prosecution? You've never seen that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Such a request never arrived to us. I mean, I don't know about the other people, but I'm a third member of the collegium, and I never saw this. I never received this. I never saw the reply to that request. How do I put this? I just happened to come across this by accident.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... the simple answer is no. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the course of your work, did you receive requests from the Tribunal to have documentation provided to them in relation to missing persons?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN MISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: During my term, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you believe that you would have had to see and sign whatever was sent from the institute?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN MISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's the way it should be, according to our rules and regulations.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Misic, I've already gone beyond the time allocated to me, and I would like to thank you now for having answered our questions.

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN MISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lukic. Mr. Misic, you'll now be cross-examined by Mr. Jeremy. You find Mr. Jeremy to your right. Mr. Jeremy is counsel for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I apologise. Before my learned friend starts I would just tender the documents I used or to have them MFI'd if not translated. I can go through the list if it's a good idea to do it now or I can do it at the end of the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's do it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Or maybe produce the list for the registrar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that would be the best.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, if would you please do that, then Mr. Jeremy can start his cross-examination. Mr. Jeremy.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And good afternoon, Mr. Misic.

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN MISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: I'd like to begin by exploring your military background in a little bit more detail than has been explored. So you already mentioned you completed the Military Academy of Land Forces in Belgrade and that your specialty is in infantry. Now, in addition to those details, you were a brigade commander during the war, yes?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN MISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And, specifically, you were the commander of the 2nd Ozren Brigade; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN MISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And you held this position for the duration of the war; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN MISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the most part.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: What was the -- what was the date that you left that position?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN MISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was seriously wounded on 19 May 1995, and from that time on, I was no longer a brigade commander but in September or the beginning of October, I was still engaged in the Ozren sector but no longer as a brigade commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: So I understand that you were out of theatre between the 19th of May, 1995 and September 1995; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN MISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Several times I had to get involved personally for moral support on the front lines, and I did appear on the front line but not as brigade commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Okay. And what was the highest rank that you achieved during the war period?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN MISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: During the war, I was promoted only once, in 1994, from captain first class to major. And after the war, I was promoted into lieutenant-colonel before I retired.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And before you joined the VRS, you were in the JNA; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN MISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And where were you based and what was your position in the JNA?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN MISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the JNA, from 1980 to 1992, I occupied several positions, from commanding officer, to instructor at the centre of the land forces in Sarajevo. Mainly in the school for Land Forces. The Marsal Tito barracks in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Now, you were -- you were formally transferred to the VRS from the JNA pursuant a specific request from General Mladic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN MISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know if it was pursuant to a request. I just happened to be in Bosnia-Herzegovina when the war began, and I accepted the duties given me and, at that time, I wasn't even thinking about the staffing issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Could we please take a look at P4970, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Sir, we'll look at this document briefly but we see that this is document from the Main Staff of the Army of the Serbian Republic of BH. It's dated the 31st of May, 1992. It's sent to the Federal Secretariat of National Defence, and we read below that a reference to a decision of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia Presidency, and it goes on to request that active servicemen are urgently sent as follows.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And if we can go to the second page of this document, please. Sorry, the third page in English and the second page in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And, sir, looking at point e, to the Eastern Bosnia Corps Bijeljina, number 2, we see a reference to Milutin Misic; Branko. That's a reference to you; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN MISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And I note on the bottom of the page we see General Mladic's name and the document seems to have been signed on his behalf. Now in reviewing General Mladic's military notebook during the war period I noticed a number of references to you. Just approximately how many times did you meet General Mladic or were you present at meetings at which General Mladic was also present during the war period?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN MISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I first saw General Mladic at the Lukavica barracks in the beginning of June 1992 when we, who had been under siege in the barracks, that is to say, the military training grounds in Pazaric, were liberated, thanks to General Mladic. After leaving Pazaric, we passed through the Lukavica barracks, and I stayed behind that column of troops. They continued on, and I stayed at Lukavica where I first met General Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You're giving all kind of details which you were not asked for. The only thing you were asked to tell us is approximately how many times did you meet General Mladic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Four or five times, between 1992 and 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And that includes meetings where he was present and you were present.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: So moving to the 2nd Ozren Brigade, the brigade in which you were the commander of, initially that was part of the Eastern Bosnia Corps, and from July 1992, it became part of the Ozren Tactical Group within the 1st Krajina Corps; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN MISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And your brigade's area of responsibility included locations on Mount Ozren; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN MISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Now in, 1995, your commander and the commander of the Ozren Tactical Group was Lieutenant-Colonel Novak Djukic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN MISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Could we take a look at 65 ter 32618, please. If we could zoom in to the top of the page, which is not very legible in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: So, sir -- it's not very clear but it's become a little bit clearer. We see this a document from the command of the Ozren Tactical Group. It's dated the 21st of January, 1995, and we see that it's a list of professional servicemen in the Ozren Tactical Group. And if we go to the second page in each document, please. And, sir, we see a reference to a Milutin Misic, major, at number 15. Is that a reference to yourself?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN MISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And we see that this document is signed by Lieutenant-Colonel Novak Djukic. Now, sir, a few months later in this year, in 1995, specifically on the 25th of May, 1995, Tuzla market-place was shelled from a location on Mount Ozren. And on April 2014, this man, Commander Novak Djukic was convicted by the Bosnian State Court for this event. Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN MISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And do I understand from your earlier answer that on the 25th of May, 1995 you were -- you were not in theatre. You had been injured?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN MISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Despite the fact you were not there, were you nevertheless aware --

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN MISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me, just let's repeat the dates. Which date in May are you asking about?

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: I'm ask you about the 25th of May, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN MISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember, I think it was on 19 May that I was wounded, so it's possible that on 25 May I was still there, that I was not yet on sick-leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Earlier you testified that you were wounded on the 19th of May, so --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 19 May, correct. So on 25 May, if I understood the Prosecutor correctly, he's asking me if I was in the area. I was. Whether I was absent during those precise days, it's possible, but I was still in -- in the area. I don't think I had been wounded at that time yet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... quite a significant event and killing 71 people, according to the BH Court judgement, do you remember the particular event occurring?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN MISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I found out about the specific event after the combat was over. Before I was wounded, I didn't know about it. I learned about it when people started talking about it publicly and when the indictments came. That was not during the war. That was later, when I was probably already retired.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please seek clarification. From what I understand, the witness says, on the one hand he was wounded on the 19th of May and at another moment he says that on 25th of May he was not yet wounded, which is difficult for me to reconcile. Witness, have you heard my observation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Believe me, I can't be certain whether I was wounded on the 19th or the 25th of May. That's what's confusing me a little. Perhaps there's a document about it that we could look up. I know it sounds funny, but I can't be sure -- I think I was wounded on the 29th of May. Perhaps I said 19th because I was wounded once before that, and I confused it too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You've given us as the options the 19th, later you said perhaps the 25th of May, and now you referring to the 29th of May.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I said on the 25 of May I was still in the service and was not yet wounded. So I was wounded on the 29th, definitely. It was the 29th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be very well aware, Mr. Misic, that if you earlier said it was the 19th, that we rely -- at least we may rely on that because you say so. And, therefore, if you're uncertain about dates please tell us, but it has now been clarified that you were wounded only after the 25th of May, possibly on the 29th, on or after the 25th and possibly the 29th. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: So, Mr. Misic, it is therefore correct that on the 25th of May 1995 on the day of this Tuzla market-place was shelled you were at your position within the Ozren Tactical Group; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN MISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And if I understand one of your earlier answers correctly, despite the fact that you were at this position, at your position on this day, you nevertheless only found out about the shelling after the war; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN MISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Now this was an incident that killed 71 people at a market-place. Would that not have been an event that you would have discussed with your colleagues during the war, during the day that you were actually there?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN MISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I don't know and didn't know who fired and whether anyone fired from that place, nor was I able to hear from anyone where the shell had fallen. It's, after all, 25 to 30 kilometres away from our positions. It's not the kind of information you can receive within a couple of days. You understand that?

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: I'm not suggesting you necessarily received the information within a couple of days, but if I understand your answer correctly you only found out about this after the war, so do you recall when exactly after the war you found out about this shelling?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN MISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I couldn't remember. Because after that event, I was wounded only three or four days later. I spent several months in treatment. After that, many other events occurred one after another. I didn't make inquiries and all I learned, I learned haphazardly and by chance you must understand that it was a very eventful time in the area and I learned about that only when an indictment was issued against someone about the incident and even about that, I'm not sure it was correct information.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Okay. Let's move on. And let's move to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mladic, no speaking aloud. Take off your earphones if you want to consult with counsel. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Mr. Misic, let's move to your role within the missing persons institute. Now, you've already explained to the Court that you began working there in September 2011; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN MISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, 1st September, 2011.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Sorry -- and the missing persons institute was jointly founded by the ICMP and by the Council of Ministers of Bosnia-Herzegovina on the 30th of August, 2005; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN MISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And from that time onwards, the institute became an institute of the state of Bosnia-Herzegovina; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN MISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, although officially it went -- it started working in -- on the 1st of January, 2008. The date you mentioned is when the agreement was signed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Yes, so it became fully operational in January 2008.

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN MISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Now, sir, I take it you're familiar with the ICMP's 2014 stock-taking reports, yes?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You said 2014?

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know. Which reports do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: We'll take a look at the document I'm referring to and see if you recognise it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Could we please take a look at 65 ter 32612.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Sir, do you recognise the front page of the document that we have on the screen before us.

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN MISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Could we go to page 11, please, in each language.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And, sir, we see on the screen before us the executive summary of the report and we read the -- in the first paragraph certain acknowledgments within --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, could you avoid touching the microphone with your clothing. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: So, sir, we see this executive summary and we see the acknowledgments in the first sentence and we see, "This report would not have been possible without the dedicated efforts of ..." and we see certain names and then we see a reference to the missing persons institute of BiH. So, sir, can I take it that your organisation contributed to the compilation of this report?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN MISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe indirectly. It was due to some of our reports that were later incorporated into this one. In any case we did not provide any separate particular documentation for this purpose, nor did we take part as the institute in the elaboration of this report. But it's our obligation to provide certain documents to the co-founder and it's possible that some of the institute's documents were used in creating this report, but we did not participate.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Okay. Now, looking at the second paragraph on the screen before us, we read the first sentence as follows: "In BiH, approximately 70 per cent of the persons reported missing as a consequence of the war have been accounted for. No other post-conflict country has achieved such a high rate of resolving cases of missing persons which has been one of the most successful aspects of BiH's post-war recovery." So I take it you would agree with that?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN MISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the most part, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And you say "for the most part." What part would you not agree to?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN MISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You know, when you say around or approximately, I cannot accept it with a grain of salt. It's no good to talk about certain things 20 years later. If we say that we identified 70.000 people after the war, to be more precise, we should say 69.000 ...

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Just to be clear, the 70 reference here is a reference to a per cent rather than an absolute number. Just so that you're clear.

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN MISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I understand that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Okay. I want to look at some parts of this document, and could we go to page 92, please. Now, sir, the heading of this section is the political discussion of missing persons numbers. I'd like you to take a look at the very first paragraph which reads as follows: "Following the cessation of hostilities in the former Yugoslavia, painstaking efforts have been made to build law-based institutions and to employ modern scientific methods to account for the missing in a non-discriminatory fashion. Despite these efforts, the issue continues to be misused for political ends. Newspapers in the region often contain inflammatory stories, stating that the process of accounting for the missing is biased against one group or the other, and politicians often resort to manipulating numbers of missing persons for political gain." Mr. Misic, I take it you would also agree with this part of the report?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN MISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Now, to briefly explore your own political affiliations, in August 2007, you were elected secretary of the Doboj SNSD party; yes?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN MISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And in October 2008, you stood for election as the SNSD representative for the Doboj Municipal Assembly; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN MISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And you continue to be active within the SNSD political party; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN MISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Are you still a member of the party?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN MISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, formally I think I still am, but I'm not sure. Since my work has been frozen from the beginning of these election, I practically haven't been active in the party or in any kind of political or party work.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And when you say your work has been frozen since the beginning of these elections, which elections are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN MISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, let me tell you straight away that twice I was elected secretary of the Municipal Board in Doboj, and I didn't stick it out longer than a few months either time. How do I put this? I'm not very skilful at politics. So, truth to tell, I was on the list; but after that, I didn't really deal with the party and with politics as such, at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jeremy, could we hear when it was that you were elected secretary of the Municipal Board twice. What years?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was elected secretary in 2006 and soon later, perhaps two months later, I resigned. And then I think it was 2008, there was a new composition, and they asked me to come back as secretary again, so I did that, and, again, I couldn't really find my way, if you will. I'm not very good at politics. So I resigned again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I was asking for the years, and you've answered that question. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: So, sir, what was -- you said you're still a member of the SNSD what was the most recent year in which you were politically active within that party?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN MISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think 2008. And even if I have been a member since then, I'm a passive member.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And do you have any concerns that your passive membership of the SNSD leaves you open to the -- some of the accusations that you've levelled against certain members of the missing persons institute of certain bias and so on?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN MISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I repeat, I am not active in politics or any kind of party work at all, especially not from September 2011 onwards, especially not when compared to the colleague that I've mentioned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jeremy, I'm looking at the clock. It's -- we are already a bit late for the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'd like to see you back, Mr. Misic, in 20 minutes. We take a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will resume at ten minutes to 2.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mladic, it all happens here, not there. Could the witness be escorted in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jeremy, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. And if I could actually tender the document that I used with the witness, 32618, document signed by Novak Djukic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's not the report we last had on our screens? No. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit P7457, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And, sir, just before we move on, we were discussing the SNSD as the political party that you were a member of. Now, I used the acronym but the full title of that party is the Alliance of Independent Social Democrats; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN MISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And the president of that party is Milorad Dodik; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN MISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Okay. Now, moving back to missing persons issues, would you agree that there is very little difference in the percentage of identification rates between persons reported missing by the Federation and persons reporting missing by the RS?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN MISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The identified?

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Yes, so the rates of identification of missing persons who have been reported missing by either the Federation or reported missing by entities within RS, Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN MISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And if we look at the document on the screen before us in the third paragraph, We read as follows: "ICMP works without regard to the ethnic affiliations of missing persons and does not maintain missing persons statistics by ethnic or other... characteristics. However" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: "Group characteristics."

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: "...or other group characteristics. However, the CEN records indicate that there is no significant difference in the identification rate of individuals reported missing by either the FBiH or the RS. For missing persons reported by the RS, 72.18 per cent have been identified, and regarding missing persons reported by the FBiH, 74.83 per cent have been identified." So, sir, I take it that you would agree with that paragraph in this ICMP report.

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN MISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'll agree although I didn't have any insight into information that would support this, but I think that it can be taken as correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's move now to the issue of verification of the central records for missing persons which you've discussed already in some detail during your direct testimony. Now, the central records on missing persons, or CEN, combined numbered 12 separate databases of information on missing persons collected from various missing persons organisations in the Federation and in the RS; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN MISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: If we could go to page 42 of this report, ICMP report.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Sir, directing your attention to paragraph 4.4, to paraphrase we see that BY February 2011, CEN combined the 12 separate databases and we read that they were collected by former Federation commission on missing person, the RS office for tracing missing and detained persons and the state commission on tracing missing persons, as well as data from the ICRC and ICMP. And then we read that the CEN is a collection of individual records of missing persons including physical characteristics, place and circumstances of a person's disappearance, and it goes on. And in the final paragraph, sentence, in this paragraph we read the ICMP contributed to the establishment of the CEN through the provision of purpose-specific computer software and data on missing persons, including anthropological examination and field data. So, sir, I take it you would agree with all of that?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN MISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree with that but it should also be noted that after 2011, some other bases were included too. The federal base of the federal commission did not become part of it immediately. During a certain period of time it was even concealed from the central records although it was supposed to be there with full capacity. It was only from 2012 onwards that became fully a part of the CEN.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Okay. You've been talking -- you've touched on the numbers of some of the records that have been verified and in the next paragraph we read as follows: "In January 2013, ICMP launched a project 'assistance in the gathering of information necessary for verification of the central records of missing persons (CEN)' continues to train and assign additional staff to MPI to assist with this process. The project was completed on the 31st of December 2013 when MPI reported that it had verified 16.300 out of a total of 34.463 records. In addition, 337 reported missing persons cases were added to the ICMP's database as a result of the project." So, sir, given your involvement in this process, I take it that you agree with the accuracy of the numbers quoted here?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN MISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not nearly accurate. In my view, the figures are inaccurate. Namely, this project led to a lot of misunderstanding among us in the collegium so what happened was that during 2013, I had to stop, ban any kind of activity in the process of verification because it all went upside down from the very outset, this project. All the guide-lines were not being followed. That is one thing, and secondly, here, it is incorrect that this number of persons had been verified. I told you what the actual number of verified person was, according to our documents. The ICMP believes that something has been verified and that is not in accordance with the rules but that's something different. This is their report, and on this occasion I wish to say, yet again, that the report on the work of the institute for 2013 and 2014 was not approved either by the collegium or the executive board because we could not agree on the number of verified persons in the CEN of Bosnia-Herzegovina and that is why that -- that is what the ICMP knows as well. Now why they included this is a different matter altogether.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: So there was a very full answer. I'm going to try and just focus in on certain parts of it. So you referred to activity that you're engaged in during 2013. Now, we read here that the report refers to completion of the project by the 31st of December, 2013. So that would take into account any activity you were engaged in earlier on in 2013, would it not?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN MISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: But nevertheless you continued to dispute the figures indicated here, is that correct, the numbers of identified records?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN MISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not the number of identified persons but the number of verified persons. I am challenging that and the ICMP is accepting this. The first 10.100-something I believe have not been verified. This is an ICMP report. It's not our report and I repeat once again, as for 2013 and 2014 there is no report of the work of the institute precisely because there has been no consensus by the collegium with regard to those figures.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Sir, at the outset my introduction to the report we looked at the foreword where there was the thanks to the missing persons institute for their contribution to this report. Do you recall any objections from your institution to the figures that we see referenced here?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN MISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had no chance for that. This was a report that was done outside the institute, beyond the institute, without the active participation of the institute. I've already said that. We have regular reports vis-à-vis our co-founder and perhaps some figures were based on that, but I cannot accept at all that this is that. ICMP knows that there is a problem precisely in this regard. And the ICMP, I don't know how else to put this, they've been trying to have this overcome but we haven't managed to overcome it yet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Repeatedly, Witness, you said this is not our report, this is ICMP's report and the data you challenged them. Now, there are two steps. The first is that the ICMP states in this report that the MPI reported that it had verified 16.300 out of a total of 34.463 records. The first question, therefore is: Did the MPI ever report to the ICMP on the numbers of cases they had verified? Or did they never sent a report?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This kind of report as referred to here with these figures, that kind of report was never sent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What report, if not the one with these figures, was then sent to the ICMP at the end or during or in relation to the project assistance in the gathering of information necessary -- well, the project described here? Was there any other report that was sent to the ICMP?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I really cannot answer that question for you, how they came to these figures, I can only dissociate myself from that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So you can't tell us whether any report was sent at all by the MPI to the ICMP in relation to this project at the end of 2013.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A certain report was sent along with this project, but certainly not with these figures. I say once again, the ICMP was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... yes, then there are two possibilities. Either the ICMP inaccurately states that the MPI reported the number of verified cases as said here; and the other possibility is that they did sent a report but that you were not aware of it. That's where we stand now. Mr. Jeremy, I leave it further to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And, Mr. Misic, at the time a report -- well, during 2013 you were one of the three directors of the Missing Persons Institute; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN MISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Now just before we end for today I want to look at the next paragraph in this document. We read: "MPI's rule-book on central records on missing persons provides for the establishment of a verification commission, consisting of three MPI staff members appointed by the MPI Board of Directors. The verification commission assesses the authenticity of reports of persons having gone missing and compares them to other official records pertaining to these individuals." Sir, do I take it that you were not a member of this verification commission?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN MISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm the director. I'm not a member of any commission. Verification commission is within the CEN. I'm not a member of the commission I'm just a member of the collegium of directors and that commission is organised by us. I take part in the organising process of that commission, but I'm not a member of that commission.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And do I take it, therefore, that you're not involved in the verification process yourself?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN MISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: None of the directors are actively involved in the process of verification. That is done by the commission that is integral part of the sector of the CEN.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Your Honours, I know we are nearly at the end of the day. I know there was a short matter that the Prosecution wanted to raise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we'll adjourn for the day soon but we'll first ask the witness to leave the courtroom but not until after I have instructed you that you should not speak or communicate with whomever about your testimony, either already given or still to be given, and we'd like to see you back tomorrow morning, the -- at 9.30 in this -- no, not at 9.30. We start at 11:30. We'd like to see you back tomorrow morning at 11.30. We have a bit of a different schedule. You may now follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good afternoon. Just to update the Chamber on the matter Mr. Tieger raised regarding the upcoming witness of Witness Tusevljak, Mr. Lukic had inquired if the witness's entire testimony about the document in question, 65 ter 1D05495, should be postponed. We spoke with the Defence, and we understand the parties are agreed that the witness can be asked during direct examination tomorrow essentially about what the document is, but not yet about what it says. So he could testify tomorrow about its nature, its provenance, and its connection to him but testimony about his -- its contents will be postponed along with what for scheduling reasons now appear will be most of the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's hereby on the record. And ... and the Chamber has no problem in following the suggestion of the parties. Then I put also a scheduling matter on the record already well in advance of the date concerned. In the third week of September, the week starting the 14th of September, the Chamber seriously considers not to sit that Monday, the 14th but to start hearings on Tuesday, the 15th of September but then also sit on Friday, the 18th of September. Time still unknown whether we would start at the usual time, 9.30, or as we'll do tomorrow, also have a later start at 11.30. If this causes any of the parties any problem, we'd like to hear as soon as possible. And, Mr. Lukic, already by nodding no, hereby puts on the record that he has no problems with that. Well, carefully looking at what the nodding of the Prosecution brings us -- I see you nodding yes. Does that mean that you have any problems, Mr. Traldi, or that you have no problems?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Sorry, I meant that to represent that I don't anticipate any problems, but we'll have a clear answer tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will wait for that then. We adjourn for the day, and we resume tomorrow, Friday, the 10th of July, at 11.30 in the morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Friday, the 10th day of July, 2015, at 11.30 a.m. 17 18 19 20 21 22 23 24 25
